narrative:
The model predicts you have a 42% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three personal circumstances. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Most students who passed had zero previous failures, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you to struggle again. The second most important factor is your small family size of three or fewer people. This actually works slightly in your favor compared with most students who passed, who more often come from larger families. Third, the quality of your family relationships also pulls the prediction a little toward passing; you described them as good, which is better than many students who still succeeded.

Even though your supportive family and close relationships help, the impact of your past failure is much larger, which is why the overall prediction leans toward failing. To improve, focus first on preventing another failure by creating a realistic study plan, using the extra support now available through the remedial courses, and speaking with your teachers early about the topics that caused problems before. Small, consistent changes in how you study can outweigh the past record and raise your chances of passing. (218 words)
